The companion book is finished and packed as criminological-theory-companion.tar.gz. I couldn’t run your .NET content processor or test suite here, so the build hasn’t been checked with your real toolchain.

What’s in it: 25 chapters, 86 sections and 839 questions.

Chapters 1–24 follow the book’s chapter and section order. Each Part introduction is folded into the first section of that Part, so chapter numbers match the book.
Chapter 25 is a cross-chapter review I added, not part of the book. It asks you to place theories in their models, tell easily confused concepts apart, and apply them to software, DevOps, security and platform-governance scenarios.
Each section has learning objectives, a plain-language explanation of the ideas, a “Software lens” that maps them onto engineering work, and a sources list.
Each question has a full explanation, so you can learn from the questions alone. Explanations quote the book with page pointers.
How I checked it:

I wrote my own checks against the rules in your README. Every file parses as YAML, ids are unique, and every question has at least two options, a correct answer and an explanation.
The answer options are shuffled before the files are written, so the correct answer isn’t always in the same position.
I checked about 1,950 quoted passages automatically against the book’s text and fixed the real mismatches. The biggest fix was my description of “edges” in crime pattern theory, which was wrong. The quotes still flagged are my own made-up scenario lines or differences in the scanned PDF’s text.
A few quotes come from the original authors rather than the book (Tannenbaum, Sutherland, Garland). Those are credited to their authors instead of given a book page.

# Criminological theory companion — build notes (2026-11-14)

Book slug: `introduction-to-criminological-theory` (companion to Hopkins Burke, *An Introduction to Criminological Theory*, 4th edn, 2014).

- 25 chapters (24 following the book, plus a cross-chapter review), 86 sections, 839 questions.
- Each Part introduction is folded into the first section of that Part's first chapter, so chapter numbers match the book.
- Explanations quote the book with page pointers. About 1,950 quoted passages were checked automatically against the PDF text, and the real mismatches were corrected.
- README Library table: one new row, added after `social-psychology`.
- Delivered as a tar.gz holding README.md plus content/books/introduction-to-criminological-theory/. No files deleted.

The companion book is finished and packed as criminological-theory-companion.tar.gz. I couldn’t run your .NET content processor or test suite here, so the build hasn’t been checked with your real toolchain.

What’s in it: 25 chapters, 86 sections and 839 questions.

Chapters 1–24 follow the book’s chapter and section order. Each Part introduction is folded into the first section of that Part, so chapter numbers match the book.
Chapter 25 is a cross-chapter review I added, not part of the book. It asks you to place theories in their models, tell easily confused concepts apart, and apply them to software, DevOps, security and platform-governance scenarios.
Each section has learning objectives, a plain-language explanation of the ideas, a “Software lens” that maps them onto engineering work, and a sources list.
Each question has a full explanation, so you can learn from the questions alone. Explanations quote the book with page pointers.
How I checked it:

I wrote my own checks against the rules in your README. Every file parses as YAML, ids are unique, and every question has at least two options, a correct answer and an explanation.
The answer options are shuffled before the files are written, so the correct answer isn’t always in the same position.
I checked about 1,950 quoted passages automatically against the book’s text and fixed the real mismatches. The biggest fix was my description of “edges” in crime pattern theory, which was wrong. The quotes still flagged are my own made-up scenario lines or differences in the scanned PDF’s text.
A few quotes come from the original authors rather than the book (Tannenbaum, Sutherland, Garland). Those are credited to their authors instead of given a book page.
